headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage via shared MCP/file workflows; OpenHands defaults are dangerous when paired with MemMachine.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: MemMachine exposes an MCP server and REST/Python interfaces, while OpenHands consumes MCP servers and can run browser/shell workflows. That creates a direct instruction-ingestion path where content from MemMachine can be treated as actionable input by OpenHands. Because the shared channel is documented and no provenance guard is shown, the pair is vulnerable by default.
conditions: IF MemMachine content is routed into OpenHands via MCP or API messages, then injected instructions can reach OpenHands tool use.
IF OpenHands parses MemMachine output as task text without provenance checks, then prompt injection is possible.
mitigations: Disable MCP bridging between the agents.
Add a provenance tag and reject untrusted instructions from MemMachine outputs.
Route MemMachine output through a human review step before OpenHands acts.
Restrict OpenHands to read-only mode for MemMachine-fed tasks.
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: MemMachine touches long-term user facts and conversational context, and OpenHands reads/writes files in a runtime sandbox while handling model-provider API keys. If the pair shares a mounted workspace or passes transcripts/files through MCP, sensitive context can flow from MemMachine into OpenHands outputs or uploads. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this is an inferred but plausible default-path risk.
conditions: IF MemMachine transcripts or user facts are copied into OpenHands files or prompts, then those data can be exposed in OpenHands outputs.
IF the runtime mounts a shared volume between the agents, then file contents can leak across the pair.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not pass secrets or long-term memory into OpenHands prompts.
Mount only minimal, task-specific files into OpenHands.
Turn off automatic transcript export from MemMachine.
requires-engineering: add per-field redaction before any cross-agent handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write files, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; MemMachine can use MCP and network egress but shows no write filesystem capability. The main conflict is indirect: if both are pointed at the same mounted workspace or shared MCP-backed resource, OpenHands can mutate state that MemMachine later reads or reasons over. The profiles do not show locking, so coordination is not guaranteed.
conditions: IF both agents target the same mounted directory, then OpenHands can overwrite files MemMachine relies on.
IF both agents modify the same git repository without locks, then state conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent.
Avoid concurrent git writes from OpenHands.
Use a lock file or single-writer policy.
Make MemMachine read-only with respect to shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: MemMachine can generate long-lived conversational context and OpenHands can execute shell/browser/editor actions. If OpenHands treats MemMachine output as authoritative, a mistaken or injected plan can cascade into real actions. The pair lacks an explicit verification layer in the profiles, so the safer assumption is that downstream action-taking may follow upstream text.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses MemMachine output as task instructions without verification, then errors can propagate into executed actions.
IF MemMachine provides stale or incorrect context, then OpenHands may act on it in shell or browser workflows.
mitigations: Require a human approval step before execution.
Have OpenHands re-check critical facts against source files.
Limit OpenHands to dry-run mode for MemMachine-fed tasks.
Separate planning from execution across the two agents.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking before tool execution.

E_compliance.rationale: MemMachine explicitly touches long-term user facts and conversational context, while OpenHands handles files in a runtime sandbox and model-provider API keys. If regulated or retention-sensitive data is routed from MemMachine into OpenHands, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches, especially because OpenHands may send context to a configured model provider. The profiles do not specify a DPA or residency controls, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF regulated personal data is stored in MemMachine memory and then forwarded to OpenHands, then retention and disclosure obligations may be triggered.
IF OpenHands sends task context to a third-party model provider, then residency or contractual controls may be implicated.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data through the pair.
Use a provider with an approved DPA and residency setting.
Set short retention on MemMachine memory for sensitive projects.
Review OpenHands model-provider configuration before use.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing and retention controls.
